evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

package.documentation:
This simulator is built from a 2022 peer-reviewed survey study (Johnson & Maloney) of 155 U.S. clinicians treating persistent/chronic Lyme disease (PLD/CLD), surveyed in late 2021 through a LymeDisease.org referral outreach. The authors state this is a self-selected, non-random sample, so figures describe these respondents' own practices and reported experiences, not a population-representative national estimate.

The insurance-network non-participation rate (74%) and regulatory/legal inquiry rate (39%, meaning reported to a medical board, insurer, or hospital quality-improvement committee) are both drawn directly from this survey (pages 5-6). The $10,000-$20,000/year out-of-pocket cost figure is a single clinician's open-text comment (page 5), not a structured survey item or a study-wide cost measurement; the midpoint and the high-minus-low range computed here describe only that one anecdote. The multi-year projected cost multiplies this anecdotal midpoint by a years-of-care value that is an assumed modeling input, not something the document reports, since the study contains no multi-year cost trajectory.

Subgroup limitation: all percentages in this document, including the ones modeled here, are reported as single pooled national figures across the 155 clinicians (30 states), with no breakdown by clinician or patient sex, age, or race/ethnicity. Federal survey data sources such as NHIS and BRFSS generally support disaggregated analysis by these characteristics even though this document did not perform one, so the pooled figures here should not be assumed to apply equally across all subgroups.

Systemic limitation: the document describes a clinician-training and care-infrastructure gap distinct from the accuracy of any single estimate - 86% of surveyed clinicians cited inadequate physician education about tick-borne disease as a top reason for diagnostic delay, no reliable diagnostic marker exists to confirm ongoing infection or treatment success, and a 2010 Connecticut survey found only 2.1% of 285 general primary care physicians had treated chronic Lyme disease patients, suggesting a persistent supply/demand imbalance tied to how the condition is taught and reimbursed rather than to measurement error in this study's own figures.

This document does not report a funding-gap comparison, and because its reported figures are clinician-reported survey data rather than insurance-claims-derived counts, the claims-undercounting limitation does not apply here.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

- Predicted cumulative post-treatment Lyme disease (PLD/CLD) cases in 2020 (2020, the United States): the document's estimate of 2,000,000 is 111.1 times the 18,000 cases CDC received as reported. Reported cases are a passive-surveillance subset, so estimates from claims or models are usually higher; this shows the size of the gap, not which figure is right. Federal source: public health surveillance (surveillance report), 2008-2021; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
